title: Collisions!
tagline: Things finally touch each other — and that is when it becomes a game.
newIdea: Detecting when two sprites overlap, and removing things from a list
goals: Use `collidesWith()` to detect when your player touches another blob
Combine `if` with a collision to make something happen — collecting, scoring, losing
Remove items from an `ArrayList` safely with the backwards loop
Connect collisions to the score and game state you built last lesson

vocab.def: when two sprites overlap on screen

an item's position in a list. The first item is at index **0**
the invisible circle used to decide if something is touching. For your character it is the radius in the `super(...)` line

warmup: What does an `if` statement do? What is a `boolean`? Name one from your own game.

p: The library checks whether two circles overlap and hands you back `true` or `false`. That is exactly the kind of thing an `if` wants.

code.label: The whole idea in one line

bullets: This works because you wrote `class MyCharacter extends Blob` back in Lesson 2. Your character got `collidesWith()` for free, and you never had to write it.

howItWorks.h: Your hitbox is the radius you set in Lesson 2
p: Remember the `30` in your `super(...)` line? That is the invisible circle the collision check uses. Your art does not matter to it — only that number does.
A **bigger** radius means collisions trigger from further away, which feels generous and forgiving. A **smaller** radius means you have to be right on top of something, which feels precise and harsh.
If your collisions feel wrong today, that number is what to change.

howItWorks.h: The problem with removing things while looping
p: When you collect a coin, you want it to disappear — you remove it from the list. But removing something from a list *while you are walking through that list* causes a real problem.

Picture five coins in a row. You are standing on coin 2 and you remove it. Every coin after it shifts back one place to fill the gap. Then the loop moves you forward to position 3… but the coin that *was* at 3 is now at 2, behind you. **You just skipped it.**
If you walk from the **end** toward the front, removing something only shifts items you have already passed. Nothing gets skipped.
You do not need to memorize why. Recognize it as "the safe way to remove things while looping" and copy it when you need it.

steps: Find the for-each loop inside `playGame()` that moves and draws your coins.
**Replace it** with the backwards index loop from the starter code. Run it — nothing should look different yet.
Inside that loop, add the `if (player.collidesWith(c))` check with `coins.remove(i);` and `score = score + 1;` inside it.
Run it and go collect a coin. It should vanish and your score should go up.
If collisions feel too hard or too easy, open your `MyCharacter` tab and change the radius in the `super(...)` line.
Change your win condition to `if (coins.size() == 0)` so you win by clearing the board.
Now add hazards. Make a second `ArrayList<Blob>` of red blobs in `setup()`, using the same counting-loop pattern from Lesson 5.
In `playGame()`, loop over the hazards with a **for-each** loop (you are not removing them, so no backwards loop needed) and set `gameOver = true` if the player touches one.
Tune it until it is actually fun to play. How many hazards? How fast? That is a design decision and it is yours.

challenge: Make the game get harder as it goes: every time the player collects five coins, add two more hazards, or make the existing ones faster. Difficulty that responds to the player is what separates a demo from a game.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: Collisions are not registering, or collecting a coin crashes the sketch. **Next step:** use the backwards loop (`for (int i = list.size()-1; i >= 0; i--)`) when removing items — and remember `collidesWith()` works because `MyCharacter extends Blob`.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: The player collects coins on contact, the score goes up, and collected coins disappear without errors.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and I added my own twist — a list of hazards to dodge, more coins spawning, or a changed win condition.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I built a real dodge mechanic (enemies that cost or end the game), or made collisions do something richer (coins splitting into smaller blobs).

thinking: In one or two sentences: what happens in your game when the player touches something — and why did you loop backwards?

di.h: collidesWith() — and why they already have it
p: "The library checks whether the two circles overlap and returns true or false."

Make the connection explicit: **because `MyCharacter extends Blob`**, their character can use `collidesWith()` against any other Blob. This is the payoff for the one-word decision back in Lesson 2, and it is worth naming so `extends` feels like it earned its keep.
Do not say the word *inheritance*.

di.h: The hitbox is the radius from super()
p: Circle back to the `30` in their Lesson 2 constructor. That is the collision circle, and it has nothing to do with how big their art looks.
A big radius is forgiving; a small one is precise. Students whose character art drifted far from their radius will get collisions that feel wrong, and this is the fix.

di.h: Show the bug before the fix
p: Run a **forward** loop with a `remove()` inside it on the projector. Collect coins and let students watch items get skipped — some coins become uncollectable.
Seeing the skipping artifact makes the backwards loop feel like a solution instead of an arbitrary incantation. This is the highest-value ninety seconds of the lesson.
"If you walk forward through a list and remove something, everything after it shifts back one, and you skip the item right after it. Walking backwards avoids that problem."
Students do **not** need to memorize this or derive it. Teach it as "the safe loop for removing things" — a pattern they can recognize and copy.

code.label: The pattern to copy

p: The collision changes `score`. The `score`/`size()` check flips `gameOver`. The `gameOver` boolean drives the `if/else` in `draw()`.
Trace that chain out loud once. It is the first time the whole machine connects end to end, and students who see it will build Lesson 9 much more confidently.

guided: Everyone opens Lesson 6's sketch and finds the for-each coin loop inside `playGame()`.
Replace it with the backwards index loop, with **no** collision check yet. Run. Nothing looks different — that is the point, the loop is equivalent until you remove something.
Add the `collidesWith()` check with `remove()` and the score increment. Run. Everyone collects a coin. Let the room react.
Show the forward-loop bug on the projector if you did not already.
Switch the win condition to `coins.size() == 0` and let someone clear the board.
Anyone whose collisions feel wrong: open `MyCharacter` and tune the radius in `super(...)`.
Introduce hazards as the main personalization task. Second `ArrayList`, for-each loop (no removal), `gameOver = true` on contact. This directly sets up Lesson 9.
pitfalls: **`ConcurrentModificationException`** — removing inside a for-each loop. The crash message is intimidating and means nothing to a sixth grader. Translate it: "you changed the list while walking through it." The backwards loop is the fix.
**Off-by-one:** writing `coins.size()` instead of `coins.size() - 1`, which throws an index-out-of-bounds on the first pass.
**`i++` instead of `i--`** in the backwards loop — an infinite loop that freezes the sketch.
Collisions that never fire because the character's radius is tiny compared to the art.
Removing from the list but forgetting to increase the score, so coins vanish silently.
Adding hazards with a **backwards** loop out of habit. They are not being removed, so a for-each is simpler. Not wrong, just unnecessary.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: Because removing an item shifts everything after it back one position, so a forward loop skips the next item. Going backwards means removals only affect items you already passed.
notes: This is the lesson where it becomes a **game** rather than a moving picture. Expect energy, and leave time for play-testing.
The hazard extension is the most valuable personalization here — it naturally produces the collect/avoid structure Lesson 9 is built on. Push most students toward it.
Radius tuning is a real design decision. Frame it that way: "do you want your game generous or precise?"
The backwards loop is a copy-and-use pattern, not something to test students on. Do not let it become the hard part of the lesson.
Fast finishers: coins that split into smaller blobs on collection, or difficulty that ramps with score.
